catalog_quote: In spans bordered by any of the terminal junctures, there is one unpredictable primary stress, with or without one or more secondary stresses and commonly alternating weak stresses. Bases (the smallest elements that may be heard alone) do not appear to exhibit stress contrast when they occur alone; the stress is on the penultimate syllable; geminate vowels constitute a single syllable and thus receive primary stress only in penultimate position: [tàangáta] (men), [mángoo] (shark), [báato] (canoe connective). Geminates before pauses are not voiceless. Final vowels before suspension junctures are frequently lengthened and sometimes stressed (N2[B]:5).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (42-page A4 scan with text, PDF Title "LANGUAGE AND CULTURE OF RENNELL AND BELLONA ISLANDS: VOLUME I"; title page pp. 1-4: "FROM THE TWO CANOES / Oral Traditions of Rennell and Bellona Islands / SAMUEL H. ELBERT / TORBEN MONBERG / Danish National Museum in cooperation with the University of Hawaii Press, Honolulu 1965 Copenhagen"). extracted text gives printed p. 21 (header INTRODUCTION, in section "4. LANGUAGE AND ORTHOGRAPHY" which starts on printed p. 19) and contains the quoted passage word for word: "In spans bordered by any of the terminal junctures, there is one unpredictable primary stress, with or without one or more secondary stresses and commonly alternating weak stresses.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In a base (lexical word) pronounced alone, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, counting a long (geminate) vowel as a single syllable rather than two moras: taa-ngá-ta 'men', má-ngoo 'shark', báa-to. Stress is not contrastive at word level; at the level of the intonational span (between terminal junctures) there is one primary stress whose placement is not predictable, plus optional secondary stresses and alternating weak stresses.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned at span level: 'with or without one or more secondary stresses and commonly alternating weak stresses'; the example [tàangáta] shows a secondary (grave) on the initial long vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Final vowels before suspension junctures are frequently lengthened and sometimes stressed; a long vowel counts as one syllable, so it takes primary stress only when penultimate (mángoo, not *mangóo). Fast Bellonese speech drops vowels (double consonants), which the authors note but do not relate to stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement is for 'bases.. when they occur alone' (citation forms); the 'one unpredictable primary stress' statement is for phrase/intonation spans bounded by terminal junctures. The authors note suprasegmental analysis was incomplete when the texts were collected. Applies to both Rennellese and Bellonese dialects as described in the joint language section.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the language of both Rennell (Mugaba, Rennellese) and Bellona (Mugiki, Bellonese) as one language with two dialects (differing in /g/ vs /ng/ and some gh/ng alternations); the stress statement is given once for Rennellese without noting any dialect difference. Glottocode renn1242 (ISO mnv) covers both.
